doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Neal Hefti's whistled arrangements in Bob Astor's band
summary: In Astor's band Neal Hefti whistled arrangements and handed out blank parts.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: had a kid on trumpet named Neal Hefti, who was writing arrangements for the band, and Bob would say every Monday he had to bring in an arrangement for Tuesday rehearsal see, or Monday rehearsal, whatever. And during the week he’d say “Neal, how are you doing with the arrangement?” Neal would say “you’ll have it in time, don’t worry.” Came Monday for the rehearsal, he never got to the rhythm section. He wouldn’t finish the arrangement, because he couldn’t write a score.
Oh, he just wrote the parts individually.

What he did was, Neal Hefti was rooming with Shelly Manne the drummer. And Shelly used to complain because Neal didn’t know how to write a score, so he would whistle the arrangement, the entire arrangement from the introduction, chorus, modulation, out choruses, background choruses, everything he would whistle, each part, and after he finished the lead trumpet he would throw it on the floor and look at it, and harmonize it. [Whistles] He was whistling all night long, and Shelly used to call him “the whistler” — he said, “he drove me crazy,” in fact at night he’d have all these parts on the floor and I would get up to go to the bathroom and he’d say “watch it, Shelly, you’re stepping on my baritone.” He says I felt like I was walking through a cow pasture there. It was unbelievable. And Neal and I were one day coming down in an elevator in the hotel going to work, and he said to me you know what my biggest thrill would be in life? My ambition, that’s what he said, “my ambition is to someday write for the Count Basie Orchestra.” Do you think he achieved his goal?
I guess so. You know it might have been an advantage for you that he didn’t get to the piano part, because he might have written something very difficult, if you weren’t a reader at the time.

Well actually what happened was he would pass out the parts at the rehearsals see, and the bass player’s name was Marty too. See? Well he was Marty Two, I was Marty One, and Shelly was the drummer, and he would give us blank manuscripts and he would say “Shelly, Marty Bass and Marty Piano.” The only reason we knew it was piano was because in the left hand side it said “Piano,” and the manuscript was empty. And I’d say “hey Neal, when are you going to write me a part? I’m trying to learn how to read music.” So anyway, to get back to Chico, I couldn’t read. I hadn’t learned yet, because I was like scuffling. So when we got to Chico’s band and I was like playing these shows © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
